item.title: Education Minister Radrodro rejects NFP claims
item.description: Education Minister Aseri Radrodro has rejected claims by the National Federation Party that he misrepresented the Electoral Act over the use of school premises for political campaigning. “I was approached by The Fiji Times journalist to respond to questions on the use of school premises for political rallies,” Radrodro said.
item.content:encoded:
Education Minister Aseri Radrodro has rejected claims by the National Federation Party that he misrepresented the Electoral Act over the use of school premises for political campaigning.

“I was approached by The Fiji Times journalist to respond to questions on the use of school premises for political rallies,” Radrodro said.

“I had responded that there are MOE policies that any use of school premises need to be on the consent of the Permanent Secretary for Education.”

His comments follow a statement from NFP general secretary Kamal Iyer, who accused the Minister of misrepresenting section 113 and imposing restrictions on community and organisation-owned school halls.

The Minister instead pointed to section 150(c) of the Electoral Act, which he said specifically deals with campaigning at educational institutions.

He quoted the provision as stating that any person who conducts a campaign on the premises of an educational institution commits an offence and is liable upon conviction to a fine of up to $10,000, imprisonment for up to five years, or both.

“Until section 150 of the Fiji Electoral Act 2014 is amended or revised, it is the law at present,” Radrodro said.

He maintained that the Ministry of Education would protect the political neutrality of schools and ensure their premises were not used for political campaigning by any party.

Radrodro said the Ministry also had a responsibility to protect the integrity of educational institutions and the wellbeing of students and teachers.

He said all political parties must respect the law and “operate on an equal footing under Fiji’s electoral laws.”

item.title: One Nation declares no assets or liabilities, lists $5,005 in contributions
item.description: The One Nation political party has declared no assets or liabilities while reporting $5,005 in contributions received, according to its declaration of assets, liabilities, income and expenditure. The declaration was made pursuant to sections 16(2) and 16(3) of the Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding & Disclosures) Act 2013.
item.content:encoded:
The One Nation political party has declared no assets or liabilities while reporting $5,005 in contributions received, according to its declaration of assets, liabilities, income and expenditure.

The declaration was made pursuant to sections 16(2) and 16(3) of the Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding & Disclosures) Act 2013.

Under its declaration of assets and liabilities, the party recorded nil total assets and nil total liabilities.

The declaration also states that One Nation does not currently have a bank account, with the party indicating it was in the process of opening one and would provide the account details to the Registrar in accordance with the requirements of the Act.

Under contributions, donations and pledges, the party declared $5,005 in contributions or donations received, with no contributions or donations received in kind and no pledges recorded.

The four individual contributions making up the $5,005 total came from Faiyaz Koya ($1,250), Viam Pillay ($1,250), Sanjay Kirpal ($1,255) and Ketan Lal ($1,250).

The declaration also contains figures for the party’s income and expenditure during the reporting period.

The document forms part of the financial disclosure requirements imposed on registered political parties under Fiji’s political parties legislation.

item.title: Heavy rain alert remains in force for parts of Fiji
item.description: A heavy rain alert remains in force for Viti Levu, Yasawa, Mamanuca, Kadavu and nearby smaller islands, with isolated heavy falls and thunderstorms forecast today. The National Weather Forecasting Centre in Nadi, in its 5.30am bulletin today, said a trough of low pressure continues to affect the western part of the country.
item.content:encoded:
A heavy rain alert remains in force for Viti Levu, Yasawa, Mamanuca, Kadavu and nearby smaller islands, with isolated heavy falls and thunderstorms forecast today.

The National Weather Forecasting Centre in Nadi, in its 5.30am bulletin today, said a trough of low pressure continues to affect the western part of the country.

Occasional rain, isolated heavy falls and thunderstorms are forecast over Viti Levu, Yasawa, Mamanuca, Kadavu and nearby smaller islands through to midnight tonight.

Cloudy periods with some showers are expected elsewhere.

Moderate to fresh easterly winds are forecast, while seas are expected to be moderate to rough.

Similar conditions are expected to continue into Tuesday, with occasional rain, isolated heavy falls and thunderstorms again forecast for Viti Levu, Yasawa, Mamanuca, Kadavu and nearby smaller islands.

Cloudy periods with some showers are expected elsewhere on Tuesday.

item.title: Seruiratu questions TRC powers, demands results from $1.5M allocation
item.description: Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu has questioned whether Fiji’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission has been given sufficient powers to uncover the full truth behind the political upheavals of 1987, 2000 and 2006. Seruiratu says almost two years into the process, fundamental questions remain unanswered about the individuals who planned, supported, financed or influenced Fiji’s coups.
item.content:encoded:
Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu has questioned whether Fiji’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission has been given sufficient powers to uncover the full truth behind the political upheavals of 1987, 2000 and 2006.

Seruiratu says almost two years into the process, fundamental questions remain unanswered about the individuals who planned, supported, financed or influenced Fiji’s coups.

“I raised this concern in Parliament last December when I asked: Who were the people behind 1987? and who were the people behind 2000?” Seruiratu said.

He acknowledged the importance of the Commission hearing from victims and families but argued that documenting their experiences alone would not establish the full circumstances behind Fiji’s political crises.

“Recording people’s suffering is not, by itself, the same as establishing the truth about why these events happened, who planned them, who supported them and who benefited from them,” he said.

Seruiratu’s central concern is that the Commission does not have the power to summon witnesses.

He questioned how it could establish the truth if people with critical information refused to voluntarily appear.

“Government cannot establish a Commission to find the truth and then deny that Commission the power to require those who may hold that truth to appear before it,” he said.

Seruiratu also questioned the Government’s allocation of another $1.5 million to the Commission in the 2026–2027 National Budget, saying taxpayers were entitled to expect measurable results.

“The Opposition does not object to spending money on a credible process that can establish the truth and contribute towards lasting national reconciliation,” he said.

“What we question is spending another $1.5 million on a Commission that Government itself has prevented from using one of the most important tools available to uncover that truth.”

Seruiratu said the Commission should ultimately provide answers about who was involved in Fiji’s political upheavals, what occurred behind the scenes and what lessons could prevent similar events in the future.

He also pointed to Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka’s appearance before the Commission, saying Rabuka had stated that he succumbed to pressure from influential figures in carrying out the 1987 coup.

“The obvious question is: who were those influential figures?” Seruiratu said.

“The Commission should have the ability to pursue that evidence. It should be able to identify those individuals, summon relevant witnesses, examine their evidence and establish what role, if any, they played.”

Seruiratu said George Speight, people with direct knowledge of the 2000 events, and former and serving RFMF officers with relevant information should be heard by the Commission.

He stressed that strengthening the Commission’s powers should not be about conducting a “witch-hunt” or using the process to prosecute individuals.

“The purpose should be to establish, as accurately as possible, what happened, who was involved, why it happened and how Fiji can prevent it from happening again,” he said.

Seruiratu called on the Government to explain what had been achieved with previous funding and what specific outcomes taxpayers could expect from the additional $1.5 million.

“If Government is serious about reconciliation, it must give the Commission the tools to find that truth,” he said.

“If taxpayers are expected to fund it, then Government must ensure that the country receives tangible results.”

item.title: Court dismisses claim over police officer’s death at work
item.description: The High Court in Suva has dismissed a civil claim brought by the mother of a police officer who died in 2018, finding there was insufficient medical evidence to establish that his death was caused by work-related stress or overwork. Puisne Judge Justice Vishwa Datt Sharma, in a judgment delivered on August 5, ruled that the plaintiff had failed to prove her case on the balance of probabilities.
item.content:encoded:
The High Court in Suva has dismissed a civil claim brought by the mother of a police officer who died in 2018, finding there was insufficient medical evidence to establish that his death was caused by work-related stress or overwork.

Puisne Judge Justice Vishwa Datt Sharma, in a judgment delivered on August 5, ruled that the plaintiff had failed to prove her case on the balance of probabilities.

The case was brought by Premila Permal, mother and administratrix of the estate of the late police officer Vinit Anand Permal, against the Commissioner of Police and the Attorney-General.

Permal collapsed and died on March 8, 2018. The court heard that on the day of his death he had assisted with four post-mortem examinations before later collapsing in the office.

The central issue before the court was whether his death had been caused by work-related factors during his employment with the Fiji Police Force.

Justice Sharma said that where negligence is alleged and the cause of death is disputed, the plaintiff bears the burden of establishing on the balance of probabilities that the death was work-related.

“Medical evidence is essential in establishing a causal connection between the Deceased’s Employment and the Death,” Justice Sharma said.

The court considered medical evidence recording the cause of death as coronary artery disease and ischemic heart disease, which was classified as not work-related.

Justice Sharma noted that the plaintiff had not called medical evidence capable of substantiating the allegation that Permal had been overworked or suffered work stress that caused his death.

“Notably, the Plaintiff did not call any material medical evidence to substantiate or prove that the Decease was overworked on the day of his demise and/or had work stress,” he said.

The court found the autopsy showed Permal suffered from ischemic heart disease secondary to coronary artery disease.

Justice Sharma ultimately concluded that the plaintiff had failed to establish that the death was work-related.

“I find therefore, that the Plaintiff has failed to prove its case on the balance of probabilities,” he said.

The Writ of Summons and Statement of Claim were dismissed in their entirety, with each party ordered to bear its own costs.

item.title: NFP challenges school political meeting restrictions
item.description: The National Federation Party has accused Education Minister Aseri Radrodro of misrepresenting the Electoral Act by imposing restrictions on the use of school halls for political meetings. In a statement, NFP general secretary Kamal Iyer disputed the Minister’s interpretation of section 113 of the Electoral Act, arguing that the provision prohibits campaign activity inside a public office but does
item.content:encoded:
The National Federation Party has accused Education Minister Aseri Radrodro of misrepresenting the Electoral Act by imposing restrictions on the use of school halls for political meetings.

In a statement, NFP general secretary Kamal Iyer disputed the Minister’s interpretation of section 113 of the Electoral Act, arguing that the provision prohibits campaign activity inside a public office but does not apply broadly to all schools.

Radrodro had said that approval will need to be obtained first before political meetings can be held in school premises.

“Section 113(4) prohibits campaign activity inside a public office. It does not say ‘all schools’. It does not say ‘public infrastructure’,” Iyer said.

“It does not say every community, religious or organisation owned school becomes Government property simply because Government pays the teachers.”

Iyer also questioned any requirement for school management committees to obtain approval from the Education Permanent Secretary before allowing political meetings at their facilities.

He argued that if political activity at a school was prohibited under section 113, approval from the Permanent Secretary could not override the legislation.

“If his argument is that political activity in a school is illegal under section 113, then approval from the Permanent Secretary cannot suddenly make it legal. Section 113 contains no such exception,” Iyer said.

The NFP general secretary said many schools had been established, maintained and funded by communities, churches, religious organisations and education societies over generations.

“Government may pay teachers. Government may regulate education standards. But that does not give the Minister the right to behave as though every school compound in Fiji constitute a public office,” he said.

Iyer described a policy requiring school management committees to seek approval before allowing lawful meetings outside school hours as “excessive, controlling and undemocratic”.

He said the NFP accepted that teachers, as public officers, must not engage in political campaigning but argued that this was different from restricting how community-owned school facilities could be used after hours.

“These facilities generate income for the school management when they are hired for any activity like weddings, receptions and even political meetings,” Iyer said.

The NFP maintained it would comply with the Electoral Act but would challenge what it considers an incorrect interpretation of the legislation.

“The NFP will comply with the Electoral Act. But we will not accept a Minister twisting section 113, frightening school communities, and using Ministry policy to claim authority over facilities that Government does not own,” Iyer said.

“Fiji is a democracy. School communities are not colonies of the Ministry of Education.”

Iyer called on Radrodro to withdraw the directive immediately.

item.title: Training empowers women
item.description: FORTY-SIX women have completed a three-week community-based training (CBT) program aimed at equipping them with practical skills to improve their livelihoods and economic independence. The sixth community-based training program was organised and facilitated by International Needs Network Fiji, with funding from the New Zealand Government.
item.content:encoded:
FORTY-SIX women have completed a three-week community-based training (CBT) program aimed at equipping them with practical skills to improve their livelihoods and economic independence.

The sixth community-based training program was organised and facilitated by International Needs Network Fiji, with funding from the New Zealand Government.

The graduates were recognised during a ceremony at Nasole Methodist Church Hall in Nasinu, attended by families, friends and supporters.

International Needs Fiji executive director Laijipa Naulivou said the program was designed to empower women with skills to support themselves and their families.

“Each graduate represents a story of resilience, empowerment and hope,” she said.

She said the program helped women build confidence while strengthening their families and communities.

“Through CBT, women are not only learning skills but also building confidence, strengthening their families, and contributing to their communities.”

Ms Naulivou acknowledged the New Zealand Government for its support through the Manaaki program.

“Their support has enabled us to extend training opportunities to women across Fiji, ensuring that empowerment and livelihood creation reach those who need it most.”

Participants learned business, life and livelihood development skills, including jewellery, macramé making and fabric art.

The latest cohort brings the number of women trained since 2024 to 274, with a target of 320 graduates by the end of this year.

item.title: Ali: Why the extra security?
item.description: THE Palestinian solidarity movement is calling for greater transparency over the security arrangements surrounding the Israeli Embassy. Fiji Women’s Crisis Centre coordinator Shamima Ali, representing the movement, questioned what specific threat had prompted the heightened police presence around the embassy after police confirmed the additional security was provided at the request of the embassy.
item.content:encoded:
THE Palestinian solidarity movement is calling for greater transparency over the security arrangements surrounding the Israeli Embassy.

Fiji Women’s Crisis Centre coordinator Shamima Ali, representing the movement, questioned what specific threat had prompted the heightened police presence around the embassy after police confirmed the additional security was provided at the request of the embassy.

Ms Ali said the public had a right to know why additional security measures had been put in place.

“The security arrangements currently in place are unprecedented,” Ms Ali said.

“We believe these resources would be better directed toward serving the needs of Fijians, particularly at a time when many communities continue to express concerns about delays and inadequate responses from the police.

“We call on the Police Commissioner and the Government to explain the necessity of these extraordinary measures.”

She said the Palestinian solidarity movement had also encountered heightened police monitoring during its peaceful gatherings and demonstrations.

Ms Ali claimed participants at vigil gatherings had on some occasions been instructed to stop chanting or remove banners supporting Palestine on “security” and “safety grounds”.

However, she said police had never explained to the movement what specific threat the security measures were intended to address.

“We also strongly reject any suggestion that members of the Palestinian solidarity movement pose a threat to public safety.

“As Fijians, we also have a right to know what specific threat has been identified against the embassy.”

Ms Ali said the movement was not aware of any specific threat against the embassy and questioned why it appeared to have greater security than other embassies that had also been the subject of public protests.
